result:
There is a kitchen I have not entered in eleven years. It belongs to my grandmother, in a town I no longer remember how to reach. I know the address the way you know an old phone number—fluently, but with the faint suspicion it might no longer work.

The kitchen had linoleum the color of weak tea. The refrigerator hummed a B-flat, which is impossible, but which I will defend to my dying breath. The window faced a yard where my grandfather grew tomatoes in plastic milk jugs, and every August the smell of overripe fruit bled through the screen.

Here is the strange thing: I cannot remember the kitchen clearly. I cannot remember the tile, the hour on the clock, the shade of the curtains. But I remember the sound of standing there—my grandmother's radio murmuring opera, the clink of a spoon against ceramic, afternoon light making everything look like an overexposed photograph. I remember the weight of silence between two people who did not need to fill it.

And this is what I keep returning to: we do not remember places. We remember the temperature of a feeling housed in a place. The kitchen is gone. My grandmother is gone. But the B-flat hum still runs in some frequency I can only reach by closing my eyes and trying to feel my hands on the counter.

We are all just a collection of rooms we can no longer re-enter, carrying their drafts into every new space.
